concepts.title: Free energy, reaction direction, and energetic coupling
concepts.rationale: This is the organizing principle for understanding why pathways run forward and how ATP drives otherwise unfavorable reactions, but no dedicated teacher deck for Chapter 6 was located.
concepts.summary: A negative actual free-energy change (ΔG) means a reaction is thermodynamically favorable in the written direction; ΔG = 0 at equilibrium. Actual ΔG depends on concentrations, so it can differ from standard ΔG°′. Cells drive an endergonic step by coupling it to a sufficiently exergonic process such as ATP hydrolysis, making the summed ΔG negative.
keyPoints: ΔG predicts feasibility, not reaction rate
Actual concentrations can change the sign of ΔG
Free-energy changes of coupled reactions are additive
ATP is kinetically stable but has high phosphate-transfer potential
sourceEvidence: Lippincott's Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 6e — Chapter 6, bioenergetics and free energy (textbook concept; this chapter is confirmed for August 25 by exam-scope.md).

concepts.title: Electron-transport chain organization and electron flow
concepts.rationale: Every physician should be able to connect NADH/FADH2 oxidation, oxygen consumption, and respiratory-chain poisons.
concepts.summary: Electrons from NADH enter at Complex I and those from succinate-linked FADH2 enter at Complex II; both routes converge on coenzyme Q, Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV. Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor and is reduced to water. Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons, whereas Complex II does not.
keyPoints: ETC is in the inner mitochondrial membrane
CoQ and cytochrome c are mobile carriers
Complex II is also succinate dehydrogenase
O2 accepts electrons at Complex IV

concepts.title: Chemiosmosis, ATP synthase, and oxidative phosphorylation
concepts.rationale: This concept links fuel oxidation to ATP production and explains why inhibition at any major respiratory-chain step rapidly compromises cellular energy.
concepts.summary: Electron transport pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, creating an electrochemical gradient. Proton return through the Fo portion of Complex V drives conformational changes in F1 that synthesize ATP. Electron flow, proton pumping, and phosphorylation are therefore functionally coupled.
keyPoints: Proton-motive force is the coupling intermediate
ETC blockade prevents maintenance of the gradient

concepts.title: Respiratory-chain inhibitors versus uncouplers
concepts.rationale: Distinguishing blocked electron transfer from dissipated proton coupling is both a classic exam contrast and clinically relevant toxicology.
concepts.summary: A respiratory-chain inhibitor stops electron flow at a defined complex, decreases oxygen consumption, and prevents ATP generation. An uncoupler allows electron transport and oxygen use to continue or accelerate while dissipating the proton gradient as heat, so ATP production falls. Rotenone/amytal inhibit Complex I, antimycin A inhibits Complex III, and cyanide or carbon monoxide inhibit Complex IV.
keyPoints: Inhibitor: electron flow and oxygen consumption fall
Uncoupler: oxygen consumption rises while ATP falls
DNP is a dangerous synthetic uncoupler

concepts.title: Cytosolic NADH shuttles and reactive oxygen species
concepts.rationale: These mechanisms explain tissue-specific ATP yield and mitochondrial oxidative injury without requiring memorization of every carrier intermediate.
concepts.summary: The inner mitochondrial membrane lacks a direct NADH transporter, so reducing equivalents enter through the malate-aspartate or glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle. The malate-aspartate shuttle preserves transfer to mitochondrial NADH and the higher ATP yield. Electron leakage can partially reduce oxygen to reactive oxygen species, opposed by superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase.
keyPoints: Shuttles move reducing equivalents, not NADH itself
ROS damage lipids, proteins, and DNA
Antioxidant enzymes limit mitochondrial oxidant injury

concepts.title: Monosaccharide classification and stereochemistry
concepts.rationale: Epimers, enantiomers, and anomers underpin carbohydrate recognition, digestion, and laboratory testing, but no dedicated Chapter 7 teacher lecture was found.
concepts.summary: Monosaccharides are classified by carbonyl type and carbon number. Epimers differ at one chiral carbon, while enantiomers are mirror images; D-glucose and D-galactose are C4 epimers, and glucose and mannose are C2 epimers. Cyclization creates an anomeric carbon, and alpha and beta forms differ at that carbon.
keyPoints: Epimer differs at one chiral center
Anomer differs at the anomeric carbon
D/L does not specify optical rotation

concepts.title: Glycosidic bonds and reducing sugars
concepts.rationale: This is the chemical basis of disaccharide structure and of classic reducing-sugar tests.
concepts.summary: A glycosidic bond links the anomeric carbon of a sugar to an oxygen or nitrogen on another molecule. A sugar is reducing when it retains a free anomeric carbon capable of opening to a reactive carbonyl. All monosaccharides are reducing; lactose and maltose are reducing, whereas sucrose is not because both anomeric carbons participate in the bond.
keyPoints: Free anomeric carbon permits reduction tests
Glycosidic linkages are named by alpha/beta and carbon positions

concepts.title: Dietary disaccharides and carbohydrate digestion
concepts.rationale: The physician-facing core is knowing what is ingested, which bond is cleaved, and why brush-border enzyme loss causes osmotic symptoms.
concepts.summary: Starch digestion begins with alpha-amylases, whereas final carbohydrate digestion occurs at the small-intestinal brush border. Lactase, sucrase-isomaltase, and maltase produce glucose, galactose, and fructose for absorption. Undigested carbohydrate retains water and is fermented by colonic bacteria, producing acidic diarrhea, gas, and bloating.

concepts.title: Intestinal monosaccharide absorption
concepts.rationale: Transporter logic connects luminal digestion to oral rehydration and malabsorption physiology.
concepts.summary: Glucose and galactose enter enterocytes apically through sodium-dependent SGLT1, whereas fructose uses facilitated diffusion through GLUT5. All three leave basolaterally mainly through GLUT2. The sodium gradient that powers SGLT1 is maintained indirectly by the basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase.

concepts.title: Glycolysis: purpose, phases, location, and net yield
concepts.rationale: The carbohydrate-metabolism teacher deck explicitly introduces glycolysis, its location, products, and energy accounting. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.
concepts.summary: Glycolysis is a cytosolic pathway converting one glucose to two pyruvate through an investment phase and a payoff phase. Net substrate-level yield is two ATP and two NADH per glucose. Under anaerobic conditions, pyruvate is reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD+, so the net energy yield remains two ATP.

concepts.title: Hexokinase versus glucokinase
concepts.rationale: This contrast explains tissue glucose trapping and fed-state hepatic handling and is a standard regulated-step comparison. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.
concepts.summary: Hexokinases I-III have low Km, are active at low glucose, and are inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate in most tissues. Glucokinase in liver and pancreatic beta cells has a higher Km and Vmax and is not directly inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate. Its properties allow liver to take up excess postprandial glucose and beta cells to sense rising glucose.

concepts.title: Irreversible glycolytic steps and reciprocal regulation
concepts.rationale: PFK-1 and pyruvate kinase integrate energy status and hormones; these are the decisive control points rather than every reversible reaction. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.
concepts.summary: Hexokinase/glucokinase, PFK-1, and pyruvate kinase catalyze the major irreversible glycolytic steps. PFK-1 is activated by AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate. In liver, glucagon lowers fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and phosphorylates pyruvate kinase, suppressing glycolysis during fasting.

concepts.title: Anaerobic glycolysis, erythrocytes, and 2,3-BPG
concepts.rationale: RBC metabolism and lactate production are clinically central applications of glycolysis. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.
concepts.summary: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria, so glycolysis is their only ATP source and lactate is their end product. The Rapoport-Luebering shunt diverts 1,3-BPG to 2,3-BPG, lowering hemoglobin oxygen affinity at the cost of bypassing an ATP-generating step. Pyruvate-kinase deficiency therefore causes chronic hemolytic anemia from inadequate RBC ATP.

concepts.title: Major metabolic fates of pyruvate
concepts.rationale: The teacher deck explicitly frames pyruvate as the branch point connecting aerobic oxidation, lactate, and biosynthesis. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.
concepts.summary: Pyruvate can become lactate through LDH, acetyl-CoA through PDH, oxaloacetate through pyruvate carboxylase, or alanine by transamination. Oxygen availability, mitochondrial capacity, hormonal state, and tissue determine which fate dominates. The branch point connects glycolysis to TCA oxidation, gluconeogenesis, amino-acid transport, and anaerobic NAD+ regeneration.

concepts.title: Pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction, cofactors, and regulation
concepts.rationale: The teacher deck directly covers PDH as the irreversible link between glycolysis and the TCA cycle. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.
concepts.summary: Mitochondrial PDH oxidatively decarboxylates pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, CO2, and NADH. Its five cofactors are TPP, lipoate, CoA, FAD, and NAD+. PDH kinase phosphorylation inactivates the complex, whereas phosphatase dephosphorylation activates it; high acetyl-CoA/NADH favor inhibition and muscle Ca2+ favors activation.

concepts.title: TCA-cycle sequence, carbon loss, and energy yield
concepts.rationale: The teacher deck presents the TCA cycle as the common oxidative hub and tests its characteristic products. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.

Succinate dehydrogenase is both a TCA enzyme and respiratory Complex II, and succinyl-CoA synthetase performs substrate-level phosphorylation.

concepts.title: TCA regulation and amphibolic function
concepts.rationale: Understanding regulated dehydrogenases and replenishment is more useful than memorizing every intermediate in isolation. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.
concepts.summary: Citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase are major regulated points, inhibited by high-energy signals and activated by low-energy demand; Ca2+ stimulates oxidative metabolism in contracting muscle. TCA intermediates also supply biosynthetic pathways, making the cycle amphibolic. Anaplerotic reactions, especially biotin-dependent pyruvate carboxylase, replenish withdrawn oxaloacetate.

concepts.title: Gluconeogenic bypass reactions and energy cost
concepts.rationale: The four bypass enzymes are the minimal pathway architecture needed to understand regulation and inherited/organ-specific defects. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.

concepts.title: Reciprocal regulation of glycolysis and gluconeogenesis
concepts.rationale: This prevents futile cycling and integrates hepatic glucose production with glucagon and cellular energy state. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.

concepts.title: Cori cycle, glucose-alanine cycle, and ethanol hypoglycemia
concepts.rationale: These are the principal clinical and interorgan applications of gluconeogenic substrate flow. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.
concepts.summary: In the Cori cycle, liver converts lactate from RBCs or exercising muscle back to glucose. In the glucose-alanine cycle, alanine carries both carbon and amino nitrogen from muscle to liver. Ethanol oxidation raises hepatic NADH, shifting pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, thereby impairing gluconeogenesis and risking fasting hypoglycemia.

concepts.title: Glycogen roles and synthesis
concepts.rationale: The carbohydrate teacher deck includes glycogen handling, and liver-versus-muscle function is essential for fasting and exercise physiology. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.
concepts.summary: Liver glycogen buffers blood glucose, whereas muscle glycogen supplies local ATP during contraction. Glycogenin creates the primer, UDP-glucose provides activated glucose, glycogen synthase forms alpha-1,4 bonds, and branching enzyme creates alpha-1,6 branches. Branching increases solubility and the number of nonreducing ends available for rapid synthesis or breakdown.

concepts.title: Glycogenolysis and debranching
concepts.rationale: The distinct products of phosphorylase and debranching enzyme are recurring high-yield details that explain several glycogen-storage diseases. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.

concepts.title: Hormonal and reciprocal regulation of glycogen
concepts.rationale: Insulin, glucagon, and epinephrine coordinate glycogen synthase and phosphorylase in opposite directions. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.

Insulin activates protein phosphatase 1, which dephosphorylates and activates glycogen synthase while inactivating phosphorylase. Skeletal muscle lacks a glucagon receptor, so glucagon does not directly mobilize muscle glycogen.

concepts.title: Nonoxidative PPP and carbon rearrangement
concepts.rationale: This explains how cells match the need for ribose with the need for NADPH and reconnect pentoses to glycolysis. The local deck supports this mechanism, but exam-scope.md explicitly excludes Chapters 8–13 unless separately confirmed.

concepts.title: Lipid classes and fatty-acid structure
concepts.rationale: The teacher lipid-structure deck explicitly introduces fatty-acid saturation, cis double bonds, melting behavior, and the distinction between simple and complex lipids before applying them to membranes and transport.
concepts.summary: Fatty acids contain a carboxyl group and a hydrocarbon chain; saturated fatty acids have no carbon-carbon double bonds, whereas unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more. A cis double bond introduces a kink that reduces packing and generally lowers melting point, while greater chain length and saturation raise melting point. Triacylglycerols and cholesteryl esters are simple storage or transport lipids; phospholipids and glycolipids contain additional polar groups and are major membrane lipids.

concepts.title: Mixed micelles, enterocyte uptake, and re-esterification

concepts.title: Chylomicron assembly, clearance, and steatorrhea

concepts.title: Fatty-acid activation and the carnitine shuttle
concepts.rationale: This is the gate into long-chain fatty-acid oxidation; the audited teacher lipid-metabolism deck is dietary-lipid focused, so detailed Chapter 16 inclusion is not claimed as definite.

concepts.title: Ketogenesis and ketone-body utilization
concepts.rationale: Ketones unify fasting physiology, uncontrolled diabetes, liver metabolism, and brain fuel adaptation.

concepts.title: Fatty-acid synthesis and reciprocal control

concepts.title: Hypoglycemia recognition, mechanism, and biochemical diagnosis
concepts.rationale: The active August 25 scope explicitly includes hypoglycemia, and a physician must distinguish autonomic warning symptoms from neuroglycopenia while using the insulin–C-peptide pattern to identify endogenous insulin secretion.
concepts.summary: Falling plasma glucose first triggers counterregulatory hormones and autonomic symptoms such as tremor, palpitations, anxiety, and sweating; more severe or prolonged deficiency deprives the brain of fuel and causes confusion, abnormal behavior, seizures, or coma. Ethanol can cause fasting hypoglycemia because its high NADH state diverts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, limiting gluconeogenesis. During hypoglycemia, high insulin with high C-peptide supports endogenous secretion, whereas injected insulin raises insulin but suppresses C-peptide.

concepts.rationale: The timing and changing source of blood glucose are essential to interpreting fasting physiology.

As hepatic glycogen wanes, gluconeogenesis from lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids becomes dominant. concepts.title: Prolonged fasting and protein-sparing ketone adaptation
concepts.rationale: This explains why starvation is not simply prolonged early fasting.
concepts.summary: With prolonged fasting, hepatic ketone production rises and the brain increasingly oxidizes ketones. This reduces the brain's glucose demand and therefore decreases the amount of amino acid that must be sacrificed for gluconeogenesis. RBCs still require glucose and produce lactate because they lack mitochondria.
keyPoints: Liver makes but does not consume ketones

concepts.title: Tissue-specific fuel constraints
concepts.rationale: The exceptions—RBC, liver, brain, muscle, and adipose—are the fastest way to reason through integrated metabolism questions.
concepts.summary: RBCs lack mitochondria and need glucose for glycolysis. Liver can oxidize fatty acids and make ketones but cannot use ketones because it lacks thiophorase; muscle uses fatty acids and ketones according to state. Brain normally relies on glucose but uses substantial ketones during prolonged fasting, while long-chain fatty acids do not cross the blood-brain barrier efficiently.
keyPoints: Brain: glucose, then more ketones in fasting

concepts.title: Type 1 versus type 2 diabetes pathophysiology
concepts.rationale: Diabetes is indispensable medical biochemistry, but no dedicated local teacher diabetes deck was located.
concepts.summary: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune beta-cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency. Early type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia, followed by progressive beta-cell failure. Both increase hepatic glucose output and impair peripheral glucose handling, but severe unopposed lipolysis and ketogenesis are characteristic of untreated type 1 disease.
keyPoints: Type 2: insulin resistance plus beta-cell dysfunction

concepts.title: Diagnosis and glycemic monitoring
concepts.rationale: Every physician must interpret fasting glucose and HbA1c, though thresholds should be checked against current clinical standards when used in practice.
concepts.summary: Diabetes can be diagnosed with reproducibly elevated fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, oral-glucose-tolerance values, or classic symptoms with a high random glucose. HbA1c reflects nonenzymatic glycation over the approximate lifespan of circulating RBCs and therefore represents roughly two to three months of glycemia. Altered RBC survival can make HbA1c misleading.
keyPoints: Repeat abnormal testing when symptoms are absent
Diagnosis and treatment targets are not identical

concepts.title: DKA versus hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
concepts.rationale: This distinction is urgent clinical pattern recognition grounded in the biochemistry of insulin deficiency.
concepts.summary: Severe insulin deficiency activates adipose lipolysis and hepatic ketogenesis, causing DKA with high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. HHS typically retains enough insulin to restrain major ketogenesis but not enough to prevent profound hyperglycemia and osmotic diuresis. Both cause dehydration and require urgent fluid, electrolyte, and insulin management.
keyPoints: DKA has significant ketonemia and acidosis

concepts.title: Biochemical basis of chronic diabetic complications
concepts.rationale: Glycation and polyol-pathway injury connect persistent hyperglycemia to the organs physicians monitor.
concepts.summary: Chronic hyperglycemia forms advanced glycation end products that cross-link matrix proteins, trap plasma proteins, and activate inflammatory receptors. Sorbitol accumulation and oxidative stress contribute in tissues with insulin-independent glucose uptake. These mechanisms participate in retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, and accelerated atherosclerosis.
keyPoints: Microvascular disease affects retina, kidney, and nerves

concepts.title: Obesity measurement and metabolic risk
concepts.rationale: BMI and fat distribution are basic clinical screening concepts; no local Chapter 26 teacher deck was found.
concepts.summary: BMI is weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared and is a screening measure rather than a direct measure of adiposity. Visceral/upper-body fat is more strongly associated with insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, fatty liver, and cardiovascular disease than gluteofemoral fat. Waist measures therefore add risk information beyond BMI.

concepts.title: Leptin, ghrelin, and hypothalamic appetite circuits
concepts.rationale: These signals explain energy-homeostasis feedback and why common obesity usually is not simple leptin deficiency.
concepts.summary: Leptin from adipose tissue signals energy stores and normally suppresses orexigenic NPY/AgRP neurons while favoring anorexigenic pathways. Ghrelin rises before meals and stimulates appetite. Common obesity usually features high leptin with central leptin resistance, while weight loss lowers leptin and increases hunger signals.

concepts.title: Adipose inflammation, adiponectin, and insulin resistance
concepts.rationale: Treating adipose as an endocrine organ explains obesity-related systemic disease better than energy storage alone.
concepts.summary: Expanded visceral adipose tissue releases excess fatty acids and proinflammatory cytokines and recruits immune cells. Adiponectin, which normally supports insulin sensitivity and fatty-acid oxidation, generally falls in obesity. These changes promote hepatic and muscle insulin resistance and contribute to type 2 diabetes.

concepts.title: EAR, RDA, AI, and tolerable upper intake level
concepts.rationale: These terms prevent incorrect interpretation of nutrition recommendations, but no dedicated local Chapter 27 teacher lecture was located.
concepts.summary: The EAR estimates the intake meeting the needs of half a defined healthy group, while the RDA is set higher to cover nearly all. AI is used when evidence is insufficient to establish an EAR and RDA. The tolerable upper intake level estimates the highest chronic intake unlikely to create adverse effects and is not a recommended target.

AI substitutes when evidence is insufficient

concepts.title: Energy density and total energy expenditure
concepts.rationale: This is the minimal quantitative framework for nutrition assessment.
concepts.summary: Carbohydrate and protein provide about 4 kcal/g, fat about 9 kcal/g, and ethanol about 7 kcal/g. Resting/basal expenditure is usually the largest component of daily energy use in sedentary adults. Physical activity is the most variable component, and protein has the greatest thermic effect of feeding.

concepts.title: Essential fatty acids, limiting amino acids, and nitrogen balance
concepts.rationale: These concepts identify what diet must supply and how protein adequacy is assessed.
concepts.summary: Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are the parent essential fatty acids because humans cannot introduce double bonds beyond carbon 9. A limiting amino acid is the essential amino acid present in the lowest amount relative to need. Positive nitrogen balance occurs in growth, pregnancy, or recovery, whereas illness, trauma, or inadequate protein can produce negative balance.

Nitrogen balance reflects protein gain or loss

concepts.title: Kwashiorkor versus marasmus
concepts.rationale: This is the key clinical pattern distinction for severe protein-energy malnutrition.
concepts.summary: Kwashiorkor features disproportionate protein deficiency with edema, fatty liver, skin/hair changes, and low albumin. Marasmus reflects severe total energy deficiency with marked wasting of muscle and subcutaneous fat but usually no prominent edema. Mixed phenotypes occur, so real patients require full nutritional and medical assessment.

concepts.title: Vitamin solubility, coenzymes, storage, and toxicity
concepts.rationale: The 70-page Vitamin 2024 teacher deck explicitly covers classification, coenzymes, absorption, deficiency, and toxicity.
concepts.summary: Most B vitamins act as coenzyme precursors, whereas vitamins A and D also have hormone-like transcriptional roles. Water-soluble vitamins generally have limited storage and faster deficiency, with B12 as a major exception. Fat-soluble vitamins require normal lipid absorption, are stored more readily, and therefore have greater potential for accumulation and toxicity.

concepts.title: Thiamine (B1): TPP reactions and neurologic deficiency
concepts.rationale: The teacher deck emphasizes active forms, metabolic pathways, and clinical deficiency syndromes.
concepts.summary: Thiamine pyrophosphate supports oxidative decarboxylation by PDH, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase, plus transketolase reactions. Deficiency impairs glucose oxidation and can raise lactate. Wernicke encephalopathy presents with confusion, ataxia, and ocular abnormalities and requires thiamine before glucose in an at-risk patient.

concepts.title: Riboflavin (B2) and niacin (B3) in redox metabolism
concepts.rationale: These are the principal flavin and nicotinamide electron carriers used throughout metabolism.
concepts.summary: Riboflavin forms FMN and FAD, tightly associated redox cofactors in dehydrogenases and the respiratory chain. Niacin forms NAD+ and NADP+; NADH is used mainly for ATP-generating oxidation, while NADPH supports reductive synthesis and antioxidant defense. Niacin deficiency causes pellagra with dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.

concepts.title: Pantothenate, pyridoxine, and biotin reaction patterns
concepts.rationale: Grouping these by reaction class reduces memorization while preserving clinically important drug and deficiency links.
concepts.summary: Pantothenate is part of CoA and acyl-carrier protein, supporting acyl-group transfer. Pyridoxal phosphate from B6 supports amino-acid transamination and decarboxylation and glycogen phosphorylase; isoniazid can cause functional B6 deficiency. Biotin carries CO2 in carboxylase reactions, and avidin in raw egg white can impair its absorption.

concepts.title: Folate and B12 one-carbon metabolism
concepts.rationale: The teacher deck highlights folate pathways and B12 absorption/metabolism, including the clinically crucial neurologic distinction.
concepts.summary: Tetrahydrofolate transfers one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis, while B12 is needed for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. Both deficiencies cause megaloblastic anemia and elevated homocysteine, but only B12 deficiency raises methylmalonic acid and causes characteristic neurologic injury. B12 absorption requires gastric intrinsic factor and terminal ileum.

concepts.title: Vitamins A and D: vision, transcription, and calcium balance
concepts.rationale: The fat-soluble teacher section explicitly covers transport, activation pathways, function, deficiency, and toxicity for A and D.
concepts.summary: Retinal participates in the visual cycle and retinoic acid regulates transcription through nuclear receptors; vitamin-A deficiency causes night blindness and may progress to xerophthalmia. Vitamin D3 is made in skin, 25-hydroxylated in liver, and 1-alpha-hydroxylated in kidney to calcitriol. Calcitriol supports calcium/phosphate balance and bone mineralization; deficiency causes rickets/osteomalacia and excess causes hypercalcemia.

concepts.title: Vitamins E, K, and C: antioxidant, coagulation, and collagen roles
concepts.rationale: These functions and deficiency patterns are directly covered in the teacher vitamin deck and are common clinical reasoning points.
concepts.summary: Vitamin E is a lipid-phase antioxidant that protects membranes and RBCs from peroxidation; deficiency is most likely with fat malabsorption and can cause hemolysis or neurologic dysfunction. Vitamin K supports gamma-carboxylation of glutamate residues in clotting and bone proteins, and deficiency prolongs PT early because factor VII has a short half-life. Vitamin C supports collagen hydroxylation and iron absorption; deficiency causes scurvy with poor wound healing and bleeding.
